conservation.notes: The Lake Erie watersnake subspecies, Nerodia sipedon insularum, occurs mainly on the lake's western islands offshore from Ohio and Ontario. It was listed as threatened in 1999 after a decline caused by eradication, habitat loss and degradation, and was removed from the US Federal List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife on 16 August 2011 after recovery; it was the 23rd species or subspecies to be delisted through recovery. It now benefits from the invasive Eurasian round goby in Lake Erie, which makes up as much as 90% of its diet.

human_tolerance.notes: A pond, ditch, canal or harbour-edge snake that is frequently seen basking on the bank and dives into the water at the slightest disturbance. It does badly from traffic on a road crossing, and it is killed out of fear far more often than by anything else.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: Mating runs from April through June. Males typically reach sexual maturity during their second year, generally around 21 months.

phases.name: young
phases.note: The species is ovoviviparous: the mother carries the eggs inside her body and gives birth to free-living young, each 19-23 cm long, born between August and October. A female may have as many as 30 young at a time but the average is eight, and mothers do not care for them.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: In regions where winters are too cold for snakes to tolerate while remaining active, local species enter brumation: unlike a hibernating mammal the snake is awake but inactive, and it brumates in burrows, under rock piles or inside fallen trees.

vocalizations.description: The hiss a watersnake gives when cornered or handled, before or instead of biting. The cited article records the bite, the excrement and the musk but does not itself describe a hiss, so this entry is an authored alarm call marked Low confidence rather than a quoted description. No recording is cited.

external.note: GBIF usageKey 5223334 and family Colubridae from the GBIF Backbone record for the accepted name; iNaturalist taxon id 29305 from the iNaturalist taxa API; ITIS TSN 174251 from the ITISWebService scientific-name search, which returns Nerodia sipedon (Linnaeus, 1758) as an exact match; Wikidata Q2163958 from a Wikidata entity search for the scientific name.

common_names.note: 'The common watersnake (Nerodia sipedon) is a species of large, nonvenomous, common snake in the family Colubridae.'

conservation.note: IUCN category from Wikidata P141, which points at the IUCN 'Least Concern' item; the whole note is the article's own Lake Erie watersnake account, including the 1999 listing, the 2011 delisting and the round goby.

range.note: 'The common watersnake is found throughout eastern and central North America, from southern Ontario and southern Quebec in the north, to Texas and Florida in the south', and the northern subspecies 'naturally occurs as far west as Colorado'. Canada and the United States are both named directly. The population found in California in 2007 is introduced, so it is left out of range.native.

traits.limb_count.note: Zero: a snake has no limbs, which is why the serpentine mesh plan carries a single head part and no legs.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: The animal is 'frequently seen basking on stream banks, from which it dives into the water at the slightest disturbance', it hunts 'among plants at the water's edge' and 'at night, it concentrates on minnows and other small fish resting in shallow water'. Those three sentences are the case for Slither and Swim.

traits.thermoregulation.note: 'Snakes are ectothermic (often referred to as cold-blooded) reptiles, meaning their body temperature is primarily regulated by the surrounding environment.'

traits.nest_type.note: None. The species 'is ovoviviparous (live-bearing), which means it does not lay eggs like many other snakes' and 'Mothers do not care for their young', so there is no nest of any kind, and the schema's None is the accurate value rather than a convenient Ground.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the two ranges the article gives: adult females 159 to 408 g and adult males 80.8 to 151 g. Taking the midpoint of both together lands near the middle of a female, which is the larger and more commonly seen animal, and is consistent with the 0.755 m length taken from the two average lengths.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: 'adult females can weigh between 159 and 408 g ... typically, while the smaller male can range from 80.8 to 151 g'. The extremes the article gives separately, females to 560 g and males to 370 g, are left out so that the pair describes a typical adult.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of the two average total lengths the article gives, 'the average total length of females was 81.4 cm ... while that of males was 69.6 cm', rather than the 135 cm maximum, because a mesh built to the maximum would render every ordinary animal as a small part of itself.

traits.lifespan_y.note: Honest gap. Neither the species article nor the Snake article states a longevity figure for this or any related snake, and this record could find no openly licensed source for one. 10 years is an authored placeholder for a large-bodied colubrid that reaches sexual maturity at about 21 months, and it is the one field in this record with nothing behind it. A reviewer who wants only sourced numbers should treat this as a gap and not as a measurement.

traits.diet.note: 'During the day, it hunts among plants at the water's edge, looking for small fish, tadpoles, frogs, worms, leeches, crayfish, large insects, mollusks, annelids, salamanders, other snakes, turtles, small birds, and mammals', and 'At night, it concentrates on minnows and other small fish resting in shallow water'. fish takes 0.5 because the night diet the article describes is entirely small fish and the list opens with fish; invertebrate takes 0.3 for the worms, leeches, crayfish, insects, mollusks and annelids, which are more items in that list than any other class; vertebrate takes 0.2 for the amphibians, other snakes, turtles, birds and mammals, and for the Lake Erie subspecies the article's separate note that the round goby 'constitutes up to 90% of its diet'.

traits.social.note: 'It is quick to flee from danger' from any approach, and the article describes no grouping of any kind, only a female giving birth and leaving. Solitary, band of one.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'N. sipedon is active during the day and at night', and the article then separates a daytime edge-foraging account from a night-time one on minnows. Cathemeral is the schema's term for activity through both.

traits.defense.note: 'It is quick to flee from danger, from which it dives into the water at the slightest disturbance' is the first line of the account, so Flee is the primary defence. The article's secondary line is that 'if cornered or captured, it usually does not hesitate to defend itself', biting repeatedly and 'release[ing] excrement and musk', which would otherwise read as Spray; that cornered behaviour is carried in traits.wariness and the alarm call instead.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement at 0.35: it basks in full view on rocks, stumps and brush and will hold its ground and musk and bite if cornered, but it goes into the water at the slightest disturbance and 'It is often killed by humans out of fear; attempting to kill snakes greatly increases the chance of being bitten.'

traits.senses.note: 'It hunts using smell and sight', which is the article's only statement about the animal's senses, so olfaction is recorded as Med and vision is left at its unset default because the schema has no vision acuity field; `vibration` is recorded because a snake hunting among plants at the water's edge and lying in shallow water detects prey that way. The article also gives a very wide gape and 'flat head the same width as the neck' for the cottonmouth comparison, which is a jaw and bite statement rather than a sensory one.

habitat.use.note: 'N. sipedon inhabits streams, lakes, and ponds, as well as wetlands', it hunts in shallow water and among plants at the edge, and it basks 'on rocks, stumps, or brush'. The aquatic/ground/arboreal split is authored from those three sentences, with the arboreal share carried by the brush it climbs to bask on.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: The animal's first move from any danger is into the water, and 'At night, it concentrates on minnows and other small fish resting in shallow water', so the site it depends on is water. Brumation sites - burrows, rock piles, fallen trees - are carried in seasonal.phases instead.

habitat.resources.note: The diet list for the feeding tags, with months from the April-to-June mating and the August-to-October birth window in which the snake is visibly active and feeding; `water` covers the swimming, the shallow-water night feeding and the escape dive; `shelter` and `perch` cover the bank, rock, stump and brush it basks on. The schema's ResourceTag set has no `fish` tag, so the minnows and other small fish that make up the night diet are carried by `small_vertebrate`, the same substitution the gull record here makes.

habitat.requires.note: 'N. sipedon inhabits streams, lakes, and ponds, as well as wetlands' and it hunts at the water's edge and in shallow water, so the animal is only ever modelled within reach of water. 150 m is an authored radius in a scene; the article states no distance.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: The species lives in ponds, ditches and canals and is commonly seen basking on the bank within a few metres of people, and it is frequently kept as a pet, so urban_affinity is Adapter; road_mortality is Medium from the human persecution and vehicle figures the article gives. The numeric tolerances are authored.

seasonal.strategy.note: The species' own article documents the mating, birth and feeding year but no winter behaviour. Brumation comes from the Snake article: 'In regions where winters are too cold for snakes to tolerate while remaining active, local species will enter a period of brumation. Unlike hibernation, in which the dormant mammals are actually asleep, brumating reptiles are awake but inactive.' A northern Ohio snake is in that region, so Brumation, and Hibernation would be the wrong term for an ectotherm.

seasonal.phases.note: The April-to-June mating, the 21-month male maturity, the August-to-October births with 19-23 cm young, the average of eight and the maximum of 30, and 'Mothers do not care for their young' are all from the species article; the November-to-March brumation phase and its burrow, rock-pile and fallen-tree sites are from the Snake article. The month boundaries are judgements.

seasonal.life_stages.note: The young are 'each one 19-23 cm (7 1/2-9 in) long', so there is no egg stage and no nest stage: the species gives birth to free-living young. duration_days 365 is a judgement, because the article gives no figure for how long a young watersnake stays small, and scale 0.3 comes from the stated 19-23 cm against the 0.755 m average adult.

vocalizations.hiss.note: Authored. The cited article records the cornered response as biting, excreting and musking and does not mention a hiss; the behaviour program needs an alarm call id, so a hiss is supplied at Low confidence rather than left as an empty call. No recording is cited.

look.note: 'It has dark crossbands on the neck and dark blotches on the rest of the body', 'The common watersnake is nonvenomous and harmless to humans, but superficially resembles the venomous cottonmouth', and the watersnake 'has a longer, more slender body and a flattened head the same width as the neck, round pupils, and no heat-sensing pits'. The body colour is a drab brown, the neck crossbands and body blotches are drawn from the `markings` slot, and the round pupil and the flattened head the same width as the neck are the two features that separate it from a cottonmouth, so the head keeps the body colour and carries no pit markings. torso_aspect is set to the schema maximum of 6, above the serpentine plan's own default of 20, because the species schema caps the field at 6 and the article stresses a 'longer, more slender body'; the cap therefore governs and the value is already as slender as the format allows.

behavior.note: fsm-ground-forager-v1 is the shared program for an animal that forages when hungry, wanders, drinks, flees and rests in shelter, and both gaits are set to slither because the program has no other way to move a legless animal. The sun window is the one judgement that needs defending: the program rests the animal while the sun is between 10 and 90 degrees, which for this species means the basking period - it is 'most often seen basking on rocks, stumps, or brush' - rather than a night roost, because the same article has it feeding at the edge by day and on minnows at night. food_tag is small_vertebrate, which for this animal means the minnows and frogs it takes, and flee_m is cut to 8 m because it dives at the slightest disturbance rather than running.

seasonal.triggers.note: Authored. Brumation requires triggers and neither the species article nor the Snake article gives a temperature threshold for this snake. 10 C to enter and 12 C to exit, sustained for a fortnight and a week, are the band that a temperate Lake Erie snake is active in and dormant outside; the article's own evidence for a warm-season animal is that it 'is active during the day and at night' while hunting at the water's edge and on shallow-water minnows from spring to autumn, and that it is 'frequently seen basking on rocks, stumps, or brush'. No source is cited because none in this record states the numbers.
